name: Yusuf Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and take the ordinary account calls at a contact centre. I left school after secondary education and only joined this desk recently, so I still check with a colleague when a payment has two dates. The wage is about usual for this work. I never use AI tools; I would rather get the account screen right first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Maja sorts post on morning shifts, and our children are grown and living away. We have roughly three months of expenses saved. There are some other centres in reach, but I would have to learn a new system at each. Retirement is close enough to think about, though I have not checked what income we could live on after work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves the ordinary calls with us, and I would ask the staff meeting to keep paid time for checking a wrong payment. A small shortcut should not shorten the call before the money is found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my present shifts would carry on. Three months saved gives Maja and me some room, though I am still learning the screen and do not want another system thrown at me every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking account calls and bring two repeated wrong-payment cases to the staff meeting. In the first year of this small change, I’d sign the group’s request for paid correction minutes on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the target, fairly steady about wages. The account can look closed while the customer still has the wrong balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would you bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the case where a credit appeared on the wrong member of a household. The customer called twice because neither short call lasted long enough to compare the account numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maja (my partner) and I would leave our three-month reserve for ordinary repairs and bills. I am not counting a new saving rate from a faster computer.

say: I’d ask for **paid correction time** with the staff group.
I’d say a **closed ticket** is no substitute for a corrected balance.
think: I think my **ordinary shifts** continue in a mild change.
I value our **three-month reserve** while learning the current screen.
do: Keep **taking account calls** and bring two wrong-payment cases to a staff meeting.
Sign colleagues’ **written rota request** for paid correction minutes in the first year.
S0.quote: The account can look closed while the customer still has the wrong balance.
fieldNote: His **three-month cushion** gives some room without implying financial security forever.
Two cases support a **shared worker demand** for paid correction time.
He retains **existing savings** and never uses AI tools.

steps.text: Keep handling account calls and present two wrong-payment cases at staff meeting
Sign group request for paid correction minutes on the rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team Steady Disruption may answer balance questions before it can put a wrong payment right. I would join the staff request for written paid hours and a human appeal desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think a junior worker might lose shifts even while experienced agents keep the disputed calls. Three months saved would let us look around, but it cannot replace my wage for the rest of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues in asking for paid appeal hours and keep practising the current ledger with an experienced agent. If my hours fall in the first year routine questions move, I’d apply for a posted paid account desk at another centre after checking its written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel. I’d keep my current job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the paid rota. I would rather know the hours now than hear that everyone will be retrained someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many junior hours are paid on the new plan, not how many messages are answered. I may be on the wrong side of that difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take another centre’s rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maja (my partner) would compare the early postal shift with a new centre’s hours. We need a bus journey that still gets both of us to work.

say: I’d join colleagues asking for **written paid hours** and human appeals.
I’d question **message totals** that hide fewer junior shifts.
think: I think **junior hours** could fall while experienced agents remain.
I know **three months saved** cannot replace a year of wages.
do: Join **staff appeal-hours request** and keep practising current ledgers on paid time.
Apply for **posted paid account work** after cuts with written bill-covering weekly wages, hours and both workers’ bus journeys; move after signing.
S1.quote: Three months saved would let us look around, but it cannot replace my wage for the rest of the year.
fieldNote: He distinguishes **paid junior hours** from answered-message counts.
He learns the **current ledger**, not a new AI tool.
A new desk needs **written weekly pay** after travel and reachable buses.

steps.text: Join colleagues requesting written paid appeal hours
Keep practising current account ledgers during paid shifts
Apply for posted account work with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours
Move only after signed offer and both workers’ bus journeys fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the staff AGI by 2028 could answer and check almost every account call. Robots around 2031 come later, and a phone job will not wait for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior place could vanish while I am still learning. Three months saved is helpful, but Maja’s postal wage alone would not meet all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d join colleagues asking for written cut dates and a paid appeal route, then check posted paid front-desk openings within bus reach. If my call hours end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after fare, keeping current shifts until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three months goes quickly when two people have bills every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must an appeal worker do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the appeal worker to correct the balance, not merely take a message for the machine. That authority should be written into the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach a front desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the front desk whether its first shift starts after the bus reaches it. A vacancy I cannot get to is not a real way out for us.

say: I’d demand **written cut dates** and a paid human appeal with colleagues.
I’d say **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think my **junior place** could disappear soon.
I know **three months saved** will not cover a long search.
do: Join colleagues’ **written notice request** and inspect posted reachable front desks in 2026.
Move after calls end only on **signed after-fare bill-covering wages**, written weekly hours and first shift after bus arrival.
S2.quote: A vacancy I cannot get to is not a real way out for us.
fieldNote: His **three-month reserve** delays but cannot solve a wage gap.
The group wants **appeal authority** as well as paid hours.
A front desk requires **bus reach** and signed weekly terms.

steps.text: Join colleagues seeking written cut dates and paid appeals with correction authority
Inspect posted paid front-desk work reachable by bus
Move on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages/hours only if first shift follows bus arrival

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to see whether other local desks really pay people. I would ask for a paid look at the work before anyone sends me to an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn a clinic’s appointment desk if a worker sat beside me, though AGI could also book appointments in 2031. I need a vacancy I can hold, not a training certificate by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take a supervised paid clinic trial only if a posted paid appointment opening exists. If the role requires a privacy course, I’d take it only with employer-funded fees and paid study hours. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare, keeping my present calls until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to inspect the shift. I would learn more beside a patient clerk than from a folder of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch in clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a booking change from the call to the patient list and ask who may correct a mistake. If the trial is unpaid, I would stay on my current paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Maja check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maja (my partner) would check whether the clinic’s first appointment starts before our bus arrives. We would not accept a wage that looks fine before travel and too small afterward.

say: I’d request a **supervised paid trial** for a posted clinic opening.
I’d refuse a **certificate alone** without wages behind it.
think: I think I could learn **clinic appointments** beside a worker.
I know **2031 AGI** could also make bookings.
do: Try **supervised paid clinic work** only for a posted paid opening in 2026.
Take **required privacy course** for posted paid clinic role only with employer-funded fees and paid hours.
Move after 2031 only on **signed after-fare bill-covering wages**, written hours and first appointment after bus arrival.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect the shift.
S3.quote: I would learn more beside a patient clerk than from a folder of screens.
fieldNote: The **clinic trial** is paid and vacancy-dependent.
The **privacy course** is required only if fees and study time are funded.
He checks **first-bus arrival** and net weekly pay before moving.

steps.text: Try supervised paid clinic shift only for a posted paid opening
Take posted paid clinic role’s required privacy course only with employer-funded fees and paid hours
Move on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages/hours only if first appointment follows bus arrival

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us ten years, but paid call hours must be written down along the way. I would ask the staff group to demand an annual rota plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still need my usual wage at 68; Maja and I have not checked what income follows work. Full thinking AI may take the calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking account calls and join colleagues asking for annual paid-hour plans. If I still need the wage and calls shrink in the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a posted paid desk job after checking its written weekly wages and hours cover our bills after travel. I’d keep my current job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later date, with time to check real figures. Ten years is useful only if I can still earn through them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check retirement money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put our actual wages, savings and bills on a page before naming a retirement date. I would not put in a pension sum until I had checked whether one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own lives. I would not count their pay in our plan unless they offered help and we agreed what it meant.

say: I’d join a **yearly paid-hours request** with colleagues while the account desk still operates.
I’d say **2036 AGI** reaches account calls before robots.
think: I think I may **need wages** at 68 if our savings cannot cover bills.
I cannot assume **retirement income** without checking it.
do: Keep **taking account calls** and join colleagues’ annual paid-hours request.
Compare **actual wages**, savings and bills before naming any retirement date.
Apply if needed for **posted paid desk work** after cuts; move only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours.
S4.quote: Ten years is useful only if I can still earn through them.
fieldNote: He does not assume a **pension amount** or stopping date.
The **three-month reserve** helps but cannot support years without wages.
Adult children’s **help remains unpromised** and outside the plan.

steps.text: Keep taking account calls while paid hours remain
Join colleagues requesting annual written paid-hour plans
Compare actual wages, savings and bills before choosing any retirement date
Apply for posted paid desk work; move only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A machine could do the plain account calls I am learning, and three months saved would not cover a long loss of wages. I would want written staffing notice, paid time to fix customer errors, and an actual posted job with a weekly wage we can live on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The customer should not be sent round the queue because a screen says the complaint is closed. Someone with paid time and authority must be able to put the payment right.

headlineQuote: Someone with paid time and authority must be able to put the payment right.
portrait: At **58**, Yusuf is a junior account agent still learning after secondary school.
He and Maja have **grown children**, typical pay and roughly three months of expenses saved.
He **never uses AI** and wants to master current payment screens first.
He favours **shared worker requests** for paid correction time as automation grows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take his ordinary account calls before he finds another steady wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid correction time and a posted job with enough weekly pay would help.
